items.title: SpaceX launches classified mission for US Space Force from California
items.snippet: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force tonight (Nov. 20), sending a mystery payload to orbit from California's central coast.

items.title: Don't turn the moon into the Wild West, scientists warn
items.snippet: Researchers are calling for a moratorium on industrial exploitation of the moon, fearing the lunar environment may suffer irreversible damage if things move too fast.

items.title: Trouble at Mars: NASA's Perseverance rover, Odyssey orbiter halt science work due to glitches
items.snippet: Perseverance has been sidelined by an antenna issue, and the venerable Odyssey orbiter is dealing with a balky reaction wheel. NASA hopes both can get back to work by the end of November.

items.title: Brains of people with PTSD have unique epigenetic marks, study finds
items.snippet: The brains of people with PTSD bear molecular changes that differ from those in people with other conditions, like depression, a new study finds.

items.title: Waterfall of fog spills over Mallorca cliffs in stunning winning image for Weather Photographer of the Year 2026
items.snippet: A spectacular sea of fog, a perfectly formed rainbow and dramatic lightning strikes feature among this year's winning photographs for Weather Photographer of the Year 2026.

items.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it
items.snippet: NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached an extraordinary milestone, traveling 16.1 billion miles from Earth to become the first spacecraft so distant that its signals take a full day to reach us. Nearly 50 years after launch, the aging probe continues its historic journey through interstellar space, pushing the limits of human exploration despite dwindling power and technical challenges.

items.title: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes
items.snippet: After eight years and 10 billion kilometers in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope heading to Mercury has captured its first cosmic observations and is performing even better than scientists expected. The instrument could soon reveal Mercury's hidden chemical secrets and transform our understanding of how the solar system's smallest planet formed.

items.title: What makes rock deep beneath continents break away and sink?
items.snippet: We usually picture mountain building as rock being pushed upward. But deep beneath some mountain belts and volcanic arcs, the opposite can happen: dense rock at the base of the crust can become unstable, break away and sink hundreds of kilometers into the mantle, dragging part of the rigid outer shell of the Earth (the lithosphere) with it. items.title: Device that measures strawberry skin's strength will aid breeders
items.snippet: Resilient strawberry varieties will be more easily identifiable thanks to a tool developed by University of Queensland engineering students. The prototype measures the strength of strawberry skin, a key breeding consideration for the Australian Strawberry Breeding Program at Queensland's Department of Primary Industries.

items.title: Quantum software matches classical benchmark for a molecular interaction
items.snippet: Predicting how molecules interact is central to drug discovery: it offers important information about how a new drug might work in the human body, the side effects it can cause and more. Computationally modeling these interactions can reduce the need for lengthy and expensive lab work, but some interactions still remain beyond the reach of classical computers.

items.snippet: An international team led by researchers from Senckenberg am Meer in Wilhelmshaven has described two new species of marine tardigrades. The tiny marine organisms were discovered in the sediment of the Senghor Seamount off the coast of Cape Verde. items.title: 'Forever' chemicals? Don't be so sure, says engineer
items.snippet: Inside the disinfection room of Baltimore's Ashburton water filtration plant, 14 University of Maryland students clad in hard hats peered up at six towering vats of bleach used to treat water that flows from the distant Liberty Reservoir into the facility, killing bacteria and other pathogens before it's routed to the region's kitchen sinks.

items.title: A fish as old as Montana—the blue sucker discovered to live well over 100 years
items.snippet: Using bomb radiocarbon dating on microscopic otoliths (earstones), researchers have found that a native species of fish in the Upper Missouri River in Montana is living up to 130 years—more than triple the previous estimate of around 40 years—and some blue suckers alive today hatched in the late 1800s, around the dawn of the automobile and when Montana officially became a state.

items.title: Caribbean corals are in crisis. Fossil reefs can help point to where corals may persist
items.snippet: The fossilized remains of ancient coral reefs often sit just meters from living corals in the Caribbean, where reefs have declined sharply over the past 70 years. Those fossils could help show where corals might survive a warming future. items.title: Ancient bison hunting site in Texas challenges long-held assumptions
items.snippet: For decades, archaeologists questioned whether Native American communities in the Southern Plains hunted bison by driving herds over cliffs, a sophisticated technique widely documented farther north.

items.title: Scientists discover twist-tunable interlayer excitons in atomically thin anisotropic semiconductors
items.snippet: When light shines on a semiconductor, negatively charged electrons and positively charged holes—empty states left behind when electrons move away—pair up and bind together. This bound state is called an exciton. When two atomically thin semiconductor layers are stacked, electrons and holes can reside in different layers, forming what is known as an interlayer exciton (IE).
